title: Why Do Americans Eat Turkey on Thanksgiving? The History
description: Discover the fascinating history behind why roast turkey became the quintessential centerpiece of the American Thanksgiving dinner table.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Thanksgiving Tradition
paragraphs: Every November, millions of households across the United States gather around a dining table to share a massive meal, with roast turkey almost always taking center stage. For many, Thanksgiving simply wouldn't feel right without it. But have you ever wondered how this specific bird became the ultimate symbol of a national holiday?

While the holiday itself celebrates the concept of gratitude and harvest gatherings, the choice of turkey as the main dish is the result of a fascinating blend of geography, practicality, and 19th-century cultural storytelling.

sections.heading: Was Turkey at the First Thanksgiving?
paragraphs: One of the most common misconceptions about Thanksgiving is that the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people feasted on roast turkey at their famous 1621 harvest meal in Plymouth, Massachusetts.

While wild turkeys were certainly abundant in the region, historical records from the event—specifically the writings of colonist Edward Winslow—do not explicitly list turkey as part of the menu. Instead, the primary meats mentioned were wild fowl, such as ducks or geese, alongside venison gifted by the Wampanoag leader Massasoit.

sections.heading: The Practical Choice: Size and Abundance
paragraphs: So how did turkey become the dominant dish? Long before European settlement, native wild turkeys roamed North America in vast numbers, making them a familiar and accessible source of protein for early settlers and farmers alike.

As the holiday evolved over the centuries, turkey emerged as a remarkably practical choice for feeding large family gatherings. Unlike chickens or cows, turkeys grow large enough to feed a crowd without requiring a farmer to slaughter valuable egg-laying hens or dairy livestock. A single large bird could comfortably feed an entire extended family.

sections.heading: Sarah Josepha Hale and National Unity
paragraphs: The cementing of turkey as the Thanksgiving staple owes a massive debt to a woman named Sarah Josepha Hale, an influential magazine editor and author often called the 'Mother of Thanksgiving.'

During the 19th century, Hale campaigned tirelessly for decades to make Thanksgiving a recognized national holiday. In her popular novels and magazine articles, she frequently described traditional New England holiday dinners in mouth-watering detail, prominently featuring a large roast turkey at the head of the table. When President Abraham Lincoln officially declared Thanksgiving a national holiday in 1863, Hale's vivid descriptions had already firmly linked the bird to the celebration in the public imagination.

faq.q: Did the Pilgrims eat turkey at the first Thanksgiving?
faq.a: Historians believe wild fowl (like duck or goose) and venison were eaten at the 1621 harvest feast, but turkey was not specifically mentioned in surviving primary accounts.

faq.q: Why are turkeys so popular for large groups?
faq.a: Turkeys grow much larger than chickens, making them an ideal, cost-effective way to feed an entire family or gathering from a single bird.

faq.q: Who made Thanksgiving a national holiday?
faq.a: President Abraham Lincoln officially proclaimed Thanksgiving a national holiday in 1863, largely due to the decades-long advocacy of writer and editor Sarah Josepha Hale.
